title: DynoSim: Simulating the Pareto Frontier
oneSentenceSummary: DynoSim is a discrete-event simulation of the NVIDIA Dynamo serving stack that enables fast, faithful exploration of the deployment configuration Pareto frontier before committing GPU time.
summary: DynoSim is a workload-driven discrete-event simulator for the NVIDIA Dynamo LLM serving stack. It models the full inference pipeline—scheduler, router, planner, KV cache manager—on a single virtual timeline, using measured engine forward-pass timing from AIConfigurator. This allows developers to sweep thousands of deployment configurations (tensor-parallel shape, worker counts, routing policy, autoscaling settings, etc.) in seconds rather than hours of real GPU time. The simulator achieves ~1,500x speedup over real time on a MacBook Air. The article demonstrates DynoSim's utility through concrete experiments: KV-aware routing improves prefix cache reuse from 0.38 to 0.44-0.45; enabling the G2 host-memory tier reduces TTFT by 19.3% at peak; and autoscaling experiments reveal optimal scaling intervals (5-10 seconds) and cold-start thresholds (~180 seconds) for a Qwen3-32B workload. The vision is to make simulation the inner loop for deployment tuning, with real clusters serving as the outer validation loop, and eventually to close the loop with continuous production re-optimization.

mainPoints.point: DynoSim enables fast, faithful simulation of the entire LLM serving stack at the forward-pass level.
mainPoints.explanation: By composing scheduler, router, planner, and KV cache manager on a single discrete-event timeline, DynoSim models complex cross-layer interactions that analytical estimates miss, achieving ~1,500x speedup over real time.

mainPoints.point: Scheduler-aware replay significantly improves TTFT prediction accuracy over pure engine timing estimates.
mainPoints.explanation: AIConfigurator provides accurate per-pass timing, but TTFT is sensitive to how requests wait, batch, and chunk under high concurrency. Adding scheduler simulation closes the gap between estimates and hardware measurements.

mainPoints.point: KV-aware routing and host-memory tiering yield measurable improvements in cache reuse and latency.
mainPoints.explanation: KV-aware routing increases prefix cache reuse from 0.38 to 0.44-0.45, reducing TTFT. Enabling the G2 host-memory tier improves mean TTFT by 19.3% at peak concurrency by reducing prefill recompute.

mainPoints.point: DynoSim enables systematic exploration of autoscaling policies, revealing optimal parameters and failure thresholds.
mainPoints.explanation: Experiments show that scaling intervals of 5-10 seconds balance responsiveness and churn, and that cold-start delays beyond ~180 seconds cause catastrophic SLA violations for a Qwen3-32B workload.

mainPoints.point: The vision is to make simulation the inner loop for continuous production optimization.
mainPoints.explanation: DynoSim can periodically sweep configurations against recent production traffic, recommending or applying reconfigurations as workload distributions drift over hours and days.

keyQuotes: DynoSim is a workload-driven discrete-event simulation of the NVIDIA Dynamo serving stack.

On an Apple M4 MacBook Air, the single-threaded Rust offline replay simulated the full 23,608-request Mooncake trace... in 2.41 seconds of wall time. The simulated serving window was 60.1 minutes, about 1,500x faster than real time.
The goal is not to replace real-cluster validation. The goal is to make that validation more focused.

A smart sweeping algorithm built on top of DynoSim would run periodically against recently-recorded production traffic, search the configuration space under the current workload distribution, and recommend (or directly apply) a reconfiguration when a materially better deployment is found.
A local improvement can shift the bottleneck somewhere else.
